commitResults.messageTitle: Added new banner, changed bot name to Bibi. Updated greetings.
Level-0 completed
Implemented necessary changes for level 1
Implemented add to list feature
Implemented a new Task class, made modules to handle Task completion logic
Added functions to write a ToDo task type
Implement inherited Level 4 task types and UI testing
Implemented exceptions for level 6 requirements
Implemented remove function
[joshmode] iP
Save tasks to disk whenever the task list changes
commitResults.messageBody:
Level 7 requires the task list to survive between sessions. This first step
covers writing only; reading the file back follows in the next step.

Storage owns the save file and writes one line per task in the documented
T | 1 | read book format. The path is built with Paths.get("data", "bibi.txt")
so it stays relative to the project root and works on any operating system,
and the data folder is created on demand for a fresh copy of the project.

Encoding lives with the tasks themselves: Task.toFileFormat() writes the shared
type, status, and description fields, and each subclass supplies its own extra
fields through the new getSaveFields() hook. This mirrors how getDetails()
already works, so adding a task type later needs no change to Storage.

Bibi saves after every add, mark, unmark, and remove. A failed save is reported
but does not end the session, since the in-memory list is still usable.

The UI test runner now resets data/bibi.txt before each case, because saved
tasks would otherwise leak from one case into the next. It also understands a
<<restart>> marker and a "Saved data" block so later cases can exercise loading.

commitResults.messageTitle: Load saved tasks when Bibi starts
commitResults.messageBody:
Second step of Level 7: Bibi now reads data/bibi.txt at startup, so a session
continues from where the previous one ended.

Storage.parseTask splits a line on the field separator and rebuilds the task
through the normal Todo, Deadline, and Event constructors, which means the same
validation that guards typed input also guards loaded input. A missing save
file is treated as an ordinary first run and produces an empty list rather than
an error, since the file will not exist on someone else's computer.

Bibi confirms how many tasks were restored, and stays silent when there are
none so a first run is not cluttered.

Test plan gains three cases: tasks surviving a restart, a first run with no save
file, and restoring a file written earlier.

commitResults.messageTitle: Handle save file errors and corrupted data
commitResults.messageBody:
Third step of Level 7, covering the stretch goal. Before this change a single
damaged line crashed Bibi on startup with an ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException.

Loading now checks each line before trusting it: the field count must match the
task type, the status flag must be 1 or 0, and the type code must be known.
A line that fails any check is skipped with a numbered explanation while every
other task still loads, and blank lines are ignored. Storage.load returns a
LoadReport so it can hand back both the tasks and the warnings without printing
anything itself. A file that is not readable text, or a path that is not a file
at all, is reported the same way instead of ending the program.

Task text is now rejected when it contains '|', because such text would be
split into the wrong fields when read back and would silently corrupt the file.
Deadline and Event validate their times through the same helper as the
description, which also removes the duplicated blank checks.

Failed saves name the file and the kind of error, so a problem such as the data
folder being blocked by a file of the same name is easy to diagnose.

Test plan gains a corrupted-file case and a case for the rejected separator.

commitResults.messageTitle: Merge branch 'branch-Level-7'
commitResults.messageBody:
Level 7: Bibi saves the task list to ./data/bibi.txt after every change and
loads it again at startup, handling a missing file, a missing folder, and
corrupted content.

commitResults.messageTitle: Store deadline and event times as real dates
commitResults.messageBody:
Level 8 minimal requirement: dates are now understood as dates rather than kept
as whatever text the user typed.

The new TaskDateTime class holds a LocalDate plus an optional LocalTime, and
owns all parsing and formatting. The time is optional rather than defaulted to
midnight, so "/by 2019-10-15" stays a whole-day deadline and only prints a time
when one was actually given. Input accepts yyyy-MM-dd and d/M/yyyy, each with an
optional 24-hour time, which covers the "2/12/2019 1800" example from the brief.
Display uses MMM dd yyyy, with the locale fixed to English so month names do not
change with the machine's regional settings.

The saved form (2019-12-02 or 2019-12-02 1800) is also an accepted input format,
so the save file stays readable and editable by hand and needs no separate
parser.

Holding real dates makes a check possible that plain text could not support:
an event is now refused if it would end before it starts.

Task gains occursOn(LocalDate), answering false by default since a ToDo has no
date. Deadline and Event override it, which prepares for the "on" command.

Note that a save file written by the previous version, holding free text such as
"Sunday", no longer loads. Those lines are reported through the Level 7
corrupted-line handling and skipped, rather than being silently accepted.

Test plan updated to use real dates, plus cases for the accepted formats,
rejected dates, and an out-of-date save file.

commitResults.messageTitle: Add an on command to list tasks for one date
commitResults.messageBody:
Level 8 stretch goal: "on <date>" reports the deadlines due that day and the
events running that day.

The search is asked of the tasks themselves through occursOn, so Bibi does not
need to know which types carry dates. An event counts as occurring on any day
between its start and end, so a multi-day event is found on its middle days too,
and a ToDo is never matched because it has no date.

Matches keep the number they have in the full list rather than being renumbered,
so a task found this way can be marked or removed straight away without a
further list command.

Any time of day in the query is ignored, since the question is about the whole
day. An unreadable date is refused with the same guidance as elsewhere.

The welcome text, help text, and unknown-command hint now mention the command
and the date formats, and the test plan covers a matching date, a date with
nothing on it, and an unreadable one.

commitResults.messageTitle: Merge branch 'branch-Level-8'
commitResults.messageBody:
Level 8: deadlines and events store real dates and times through the new
TaskDateTime class, are displayed as MMM dd yyyy, and can be queried for a
single date with the on command.

commitResults.messageTitle: Extract a Ui class for all console interaction
commitResults.messageBody:
First step towards the A-MoreOOP target. Bibi was the only class that touched
System.in and System.out, and that responsibility is now Ui's.

Ui owns the mechanics of the conversation: the "You: " prompt, the divider
lines, the "Bibi: " prefix, task numbering, and the fixed screens (welcome,
help, goodbye). Wording specific to one operation is still passed in by the
caller, so adding a command later does not mean adding a method to Ui. That
keeps Ui from becoming a dumping ground of one method per message while still
making it the single place that writes to the console.

Two small fixes came with the move:

- Reaching the end of the input now counts as "bye" instead of throwing
  NoSuchElementException. Piped input that omits a final bye no longer crashes.
- markTask and unmarkTask dropped a null check on the result of findTask, which
  can never be null because findTask throws instead.

Behaviour is otherwise unchanged, which the 15 UI tests confirm.

commitResults.messageTitle: Give Storage and TaskList clearer responsibilities
commitResults.messageBody:
Second step towards A-MoreOOP, preparing for the Parser and Command classes.

Storage now reads and writes plain List<Task> instead of TaskList. Saving and
loading files has no reason to know how the running program holds its tasks, and
the narrower interface means Storage can be tested with an ordinary ArrayList.

TaskList gains a constructor that takes an existing list, so a loaded file
becomes a task list in one step rather than by adding tasks one at a time. The
tasks are copied, so the caller's list cannot be changed underneath it.

The save-file location moved out of Storage and into Bibi, which is the class
that composes the application. Storage no longer decides where it lives, it just
uses the path it is given, and there is a single place to look for the path.

Behaviour is unchanged; the 15 UI tests confirm it.

commitResults.messageTitle: Replace the command if-else chain with Parser and Command classes
commitResults.messageBody:
Third step of A-MoreOOP, covering the stretch goal in the same move because the
Parser has to return something, and a Command is the natural thing to return.

Parser now owns every command word and its syntax, and hands back a finished
Command. It resolves arguments while parsing, so "deadline ... /by ..." becomes
a built Deadline and "mark 2" becomes an int. A command can therefore assume its
input is already sound and has no parsing left to do.

Command is abstract with execute(tasks, ui, storage) and isExit(). The nine
subclasses are Add, List, Mark, Unmark, Delete, On, Help and Exit. AddCommand
covers all three task types because Parser has already built the task, so no
separate AddTodoCommand and friends are needed.

Saving after a change lives in Command.saveTasks, so the four commands that
change the list all save the same way and report a failed save the same way,
without failing the command itself.

Bibi is now an object rather than a bag of static methods. It holds ui, storage
and tasks, and run() is the short loop from the target design. Loading happens
in run() rather than the constructor because it speaks to the user and the
greeting should come first.

Two visible changes:

- Divider lines are now printed once per command by the loop, instead of by each
  operation. Commands that previously showed none, such as mark and errors, are
  now wrapped consistently.
- "help" works on its own. The old router only matched "help " with a trailing
  space, so bare "help" fell through to the unknown-command message. Writing
  that special case back deliberately made no sense while rewriting the
  dispatch, since every other command word matches both forms.

All 16 UI tests pass, including a new one pinning the help output.

commitResults.messageTitle: Merge branch 'branch-A-MoreOOP'
commitResults.messageBody:
A-MoreOOP: extract Ui, Parser and a Command hierarchy alongside the existing
Storage and TaskList, so Bibi only wires the parts together and runs the loop.

commitResults.messageTitle: Organize classes into bibi, bibi.task and bibi.command packages
commitResults.messageBody:
A-Packages, taking the stretch goal since eighteen classes are more than one
folder should hold.

The split follows the roles established in A-MoreOOP:

- bibi: Bibi, Ui, Parser, Storage, BibiException. The application itself and the
  parts that connect it to the outside world.
- bibi.task: Task, Todo, Deadline, Event, TaskList, TaskDateTime. What a task is
  and how a collection of them behaves, with no knowledge of console or files.
- bibi.command: Command and its eight subclasses. What the user can ask for.

src/main/java stays the source root, and the folders under it mirror the package
names, as the increment requires.

bibi.task came out of this as the only package that depends on nothing but
BibiException, which is a good sign the boundary is in the right place. The
bibi and bibi.command packages do depend on each other, since Parser builds
commands while commands need Ui and Storage. That cycle is inherent to the
Command pattern here and is not worth breaking with extra interfaces at this
size.

Members already had the visibility they needed, so no access modifiers changed:
the protected hooks on Task are only used by its subclasses in bibi.task, and
everything reached across a package boundary was already public.

The UI test runner now compiles recursively and runs bibi.Bibi, and the README
points at the new location of the main class. All 16 UI tests pass.

Verified that "gradlew compileJava" and "gradlew run" both work, that the app
saves to ./data/bibi.txt relative to the project root under Gradle, and that the
16 UI tests still pass. The UI test runner still compiles with javac directly,
which is quicker than going through Gradle for every case and keeps the two
checks independent.

commitResults.messageTitle: Add JUnit tests and make date parsing strict
commitResults.messageBody:
A-JUnit. 73 tests across five classes, run with "gradlew test".

Coverage follows the top ~50% highest-value methods rather than everything:

- ParserTest (20): every command word, mixed case, a command word that is only
  a prefix of another word, and each way a command can be malformed.
- StorageTest (13): the exact saved layout, a save and load round trip for all
  three task types, a missing file, a missing parent folder, blank lines, each
  kind of damaged line, and a path that is a folder rather than a file.
- TaskDateTimeTest (18): each accepted input format, formatting, storage round
  trips, and date comparison.
- TaskListTest (10): one-based numbering and its boundaries, defensive copying,
  and the unmodifiable view.
- TaskTest (12): display form, save form, occursOn, and every validation rule.

Left untested on purpose: Ui, which only writes to the console, and the thin
Command subclasses, whose behaviour is already covered through Parser and the
UI test plan.

The tests found one real bug. Java resolves dates leniently by default, so
"2019-02-30" was quietly accepted as 28 February rather than refused. The
parsing formatters now use ResolverStyle.STRICT, which required changing the
year pattern from yyyy to uuuu because the former means year-within-era and
cannot be resolved strictly on its own. A mistyped date is now reported instead
of silently becoming a different date.

AGENTS.md records the 50% coverage target, the naming convention, and that the
tests must be updated alongside each code change to stay within it.

The 16 UI tests still pass.

commitResults.messageTitle: Document building and running the fat JAR

instructions.

Verified the scenario the increment describes: "gradlew shadowJar" produces
build/libs/bibi.jar, and copying that one file into an empty folder and running
"java -jar bibi.jar" there works with nothing else installed. The run creates
its own data/bibi.txt in that folder and a second run restores the tasks, which
confirms the relative, operating-system independent save path behaves correctly
once the app is distributed rather than run from the project.

build/ is already ignored, so the JAR is not committed. The README now explains
how to create, locate, and run it, and points at a GitHub release as the way to
publish it.

commitResults.messageTitle: Add header comments to all remaining public members
commitResults.messageBody:
Fifteen overriding methods carried no header comment: execute in each of the
eight command classes, isExit in ExitCommand, and getTypeCode and getDetails in
the three task types. Anyone reading a command class had to open Command to
learn what it does.

Each now has a summary describing what that particular class does, matching the
summary-only style the existing overrides already use. Repeating the inherited
@param tags on nine identical signatures would have added noise without adding
information.

Running the javadoc tool for the first time also exposed defects that were
invisible while compiling:

- Four {@link} references broke during A-Packages and had gone unnoticed, since
  a broken link is a javadoc error rather than a compile error. Parser, TaskList
  and Storage are now linked by qualified name with a short label, because the
  referring classes have no reason to import them just for a comment.
- Five classes relied on an implicit public constructor that no comment could
  describe. The three command classes and Command now declare documented
  constructors. Parser instead declares a private one, since it holds only
  static helpers and was never meant to be instantiated.

The javadoc task now completes with no errors and no warnings. All 73 JUnit
tests and 16 UI tests still pass.

commitResults.messageTitle: Comply with the SE-EDU Java coding standard
commitResults.messageBody:
The project already shipped config/checkstyle/checkstyle.xml, which
encodes the SE-EDU intermediate standard, but nothing ever ran it. The
code had therefore drifted from the standard with no way to notice.

The Gradle checkstyle plugin now applies that config, which makes
compliance verifiable rather than a matter of opinion. Its first run
reported 78 violations of three rules:

* Import order, 59 cases. Imports must be grouped as static, java, org,
  com, then this project's own classes, separated by blank lines. Almost
  every file was wrong, because imports had only ever been sorted
  alphabetically.
* Indentation, 13 cases. The case labels of the switch expression in
  Storage.parseTask sat level with the switch instead of indented
  inside it.
* Separator wrap, 6 cases. Six wrapped assertThrows calls started a line
  with the lambda's opening parenthesis, which the standard forbids.

All are fixed, and checkstyleMain and checkstyleTest now pass. The 73
JUnit tests and 16 UI tests still pass, confirming that every change was
presentational and none altered behaviour.

commitResults.messageTitle: Add seedu-java-coding-standard skill
commitResults.messageBody:

one-off cleanup, so the rules need to be readable without visiting the

The skill records the naming, layout, statement, and comment rules, and

whether a name is a good name, and whether a comment is worth reading.

commitResults.messageBody:
Commit messages in this repository had no agreed shape, and the SE-EDU

The skill records the subject line rules, the body wrapping and content
rules, and the branch naming format, plus a short checklist to run
through before committing. It notes that the course increment branches
keep their prescribed names rather than the kebab-case convention,
because the grading scripts match on those exact names.

commitResults.messageTitle: Mandate the coding and commit standards in AGENTS.md
commitResults.messageBody:
The two new skills describe the standards but nothing yet obliged anyone
to use them, so a future change could silently ignore both.

AGENTS.md now requires the Java coding standard for all code and the Git
conventions for all commit messages, names the skill that carries each,
and states that a change is unfinished while checkstyle reports
violations.

commitResults.messageTitle: Add a find command to search task descriptions
commitResults.messageBody:
A user with a long list had no way to locate a task except to read the
whole list, which gets steadily worse as the list grows.

"find <keyword>" now shows every task whose description contains the
keyword. Two decisions worth recording:

* The match ignores case and matches any substring, so "find book"
  finds "Read Book" and "find boo" finds both. A user searching for a
  task they half remember is better served by too many results than by
  a miss on capitalisation.
* Only the description is searched, not the dates. Searching dates as
  text would make "find 2019" behave unpredictably next to the on
  command, which already answers date questions properly.

Matches keep the number they hold in the full list rather than being
renumbered from one, matching what the on command already does, so a
task found this way can be marked or removed without listing first.

Task answers hasKeyword itself, which keeps the description private and
means neither Parser nor the command needs to reach inside a task.

Covered by eight new JUnit tests and one new UI test case. Test 6 was
updated because find now appears in the unknown-command hint.

commitResults.messageTitle: Merge branch 'branch-A-CodingStandard'
Merge branch 'branch-Level-9'
commitResults.messageBody:
Level-9: find <keyword> searches task descriptions.

Git merged all three branches without a textual conflict, but this merge
still needed a fix that no tool reported.

branch-Level-9 was cut before branch-A-JavaDoc landed, so FindCommand
was written to the standard of the time and left its execute method
without a header comment. That breaks the invariant A-JavaDoc
established, that every non-private member is documented. Neither the
compiler nor checkstyle objects, because the config deliberately exempts
@Override methods, so the regression was invisible until the Javadoc
audit was rerun. The comment is added here as part of resolving the
merge, rather than in a follow-up commit, so master is never in a state
that contradicts A-JavaDoc.

The import ordering that A-CodingStandard introduced survived the merge
by luck rather than design: the find imports happened to be inserted at
alphabetically correct positions inside groups that already existed.

Verified on the merged result: checkstyle clean, javadoc clean, 81 JUnit
tests and 17 UI tests passing.

the two assistants used in this project could read them. They are now
duplicated under .claude/skills, and each copy carries a note naming its

test-ui was deliberately not duplicated. It carries a 160 line Python
script, and two copies of a script that must stay in step is a worse
trade than running it from its existing path.

recording here: it contained a syntax error. A comma was missing before
the java.checkstyle keys, so the file did not parse and none of its
settings applied, including the checkstyle configuration that was meant
to surface violations while editing. It has been rewritten with valid
JSON, the six editor settings from the SE-EDU VS Code guide, rulers at
110 and 120 to make the line limits visible, and Gradle import enabled.
The java.project.sourcePaths and java.project.outputPath entries were
dropped, since they apply only to unmanaged folders and have been inert
since this became a Gradle project.

commitResults.messageTitle: Make Checkstyle warnings fail the build
commitResults.messageBody:
Checkstyle has been configured since A-CodingStandard, but it was only
half enforcing the standard. Most rules in the SE-EDU config carry
severity "warning", and a Gradle Checkstyle task fails on errors alone,
so every warning-level rule was reported to the console and then
ignored. A build with style violations still went green, which is the
same as not having those rules at all.

Setting maxWarnings to 0 makes them binding. Confirmed by adding a
ParenPad violation, a warning-level rule, to Ui: the build passed
before this change and fails after it, naming the file, line and rule.

The source needed no fixes; main and test are already clean at every
severity, which is why the tightening could be done in one step rather
than alongside a round of corrections.

The README gains a section on running Checkstyle on its own, on where
the HTML report lands, and on why maxWarnings is set, since that last
point is the kind of thing that gets loosened later by someone who does
not know what it was for.

commitResults.messageTitle: Add a JavaFX GUI
commitResults.messageBody:
Bibi could only be used from a console, which suits neither the way most
people expect to use a task app nor the way it will be demonstrated.

The window is built with JavaFX from MainWindow.fxml, with each turn of
the conversation shown as a DialogBox: the speaker's picture beside what
they said, mirrored so the two sides of the conversation are easy to
tell apart.

None of the command handling was rewritten for it. Ui now sends every
line through one private method that either prints it or collects it,
and Bibi grew getGreeting and getResponse, which turn the collector on
and hand back the words. The GUI therefore drives exactly the same
parser, commands, task list and storage as the console, so the two
interfaces cannot drift apart. Two small differences are deliberate:
the "Bibi:" prefix is dropped when collecting, because the picture
already says who is speaking, and the banner moved to its own method
because letters drawn from spaced characters only line up in a
fixed-width font.

The console interface is kept rather than replaced. The scripted UI
tests drive it, and a console is far easier to feed a script than a
window is. It now has its own Gradle task, runCli, since gradle run
belongs to the GUI.

Launching goes through Launcher, which does not extend Application.
JavaFX refuses to start from a class that does, when its runtime is on
the classpath rather than the module path, which is how this project
supplies it. That is not a theoretical worry: an early version of the
harness used to check this work failed with exactly that error.

The JavaFX dependencies name every platform's natives, not just the one
the build happens to run on, following the sample build file in the
JavaFX tutorial. A fat JAR built anywhere then runs everywhere, which is
the whole point of shipping one.

Two things outside src had to move with it. The UI test script compiled
every source file it could find, which would now pull in classes that
need JavaFX on the classpath, so it compiles the console entry point and
lets javac follow only what that reaches. The test plan gains a note on
what those cases do and do not cover once there are two interfaces.

Verified: 17 UI tests and 90 JUnit tests pass, checkstyle is clean at
zero tolerated warnings, and the packaged JAR opens the window and still
runs the console through bibi.Bibi.

commitResults.messageTitle: Use varargs where a list is written out in place
commitResults.messageBody:
Three places took a fixed run of values and made the caller wrap or
repeat them. Varargs suits each, and nothing else in the codebase was
changed simply to use the feature.

TaskDateTime declared its accepted formats as a list of separately
wrapped strictFormat calls. strictFormats now takes the patterns as
varargs and returns the whole group, so each set of accepted formats
reads as the list of patterns it actually is.

Ui.showDetail takes the lines as varargs. showHelp used to call it
eleven times in a row, which buried the one thing worth reading, the
commands themselves, in repeated boilerplate; it is now one call listing
them. Callers with a single line to show are unaffected, and the loop in

commitResults.messageTitle: Document internal assumptions with assertions
commitResults.messageBody:
Several places in the code rely on a condition that an earlier line has
already guaranteed. Those assumptions were only visible to a reader
willing to trace the call, and breaking one produced a failure far from
its cause: an IndexOutOfBoundsException from inside TaskList, a stale
reply in a GUI bubble, or a NullPointerException swallowed by a JavaFX
event handler.

Nine assert statements now state them, each where the assumption is
relied on rather than where it is established:

- TaskList.toIndex, that the returned index is in range, since every
  caller uses it to index the list directly.
- Task.toFileFormat, that the description holds no field separator,
  which construction rejects but which would otherwise corrupt the save
  file and only fail on the next load.
- Ui.takeCapturedText, that a capture was started, because otherwise it
  quietly returns the previous capture instead of failing.
- Ui.write, that the line is not null, which would print as "null".
- Storage.parseTask, that three fields were read, which is what makes
  the fixed field reads below it safe.
- Bibi.getResponse, that the command is not null and that a reply was
  actually produced, since a silent command would show as an empty
  bubble with no hint of what went wrong.
- Bibi.loadTasks, that storage was set.
- MainWindow.handleUserInput, that setBibi ran before the window took
  input.

User input is deliberately not asserted anywhere. Bad input is expected
and is reported through BibiException; assertions are for conditions the
program itself is responsible for, and disabling them must never change
what the user sees.

The run and runCli tasks now set enableAssertions, because the JVM
disables assertions by default and Gradle leaves them off for JavaExec
tasks, which would have left every one of these as dead text outside the
test run. Confirmed enabled by a temporary test that expected an
AssertionError from takeCapturedText and got one.

commitResults.messageTitle: Use streams where the code already describes a pipeline
commitResults.messageBody:
Three places were already doing what a stream expresses, spelled out as
loops with accumulator variables.

adding one encoded task at a time. That is a one-to-one mapping, and now
says so.

FindCommand and OnCommand each walked the whole list carrying a hasMatch
flag whose only job was to decide, on the fly, whether the heading had
been shown yet. Both now work out which tasks qualify first and show
them afterwards, which separates the question being asked from the way
its answer is displayed, and removes the flag along with the ordering
subtlety it carried.

Those two stream over the task numbers rather than over the tasks. The
number a task carries in the full list is part of what is being shown,
because a match can be marked or removed by that number without listing
everything first, and filtering a stream of tasks would throw the
position away. IntStream.rangeClosed keeps it.

Storage.load is deliberately left as a loop. It reads a line number,
accumulates tasks and warnings at once, and keeps going after a bad
line, so a stream would need side effects on two collections and would
be harder to follow, not easier.

Output is unchanged, including the order in which the heading and the
matches appear. Verified by the 17 scripted UI tests and the JUnit
suite.

commitResults.messageTitle: Run the build on GitHub Actions
commitResults.messageBody:
Every check this project has could only be run by someone who remembered
to run it. Nothing stopped a branch being pushed, or a pull request
being merged, with failing tests or a checkstyle violation in it, and
nothing checked that the code still built on an operating system other
than the author's.

The workflow runs on every push and every pull request, across Linux,
macOS and Windows. Three platforms are worth the minutes here because
this project ships a JavaFX application whose dependencies are chosen
per platform; a mistake in that part of the build would show up nowhere
else.

The steps are the ones a contributor would run by hand: gradle check,
which covers the JUnit tests and checkstyle, then the scripted console
tests, then shadowJar to confirm the distributable JAR still assembles.
The scripted tests run on Linux alone, since they are platform
independent and running them three times would cost time to learn
nothing.

Two details worth recording. Each step runs under bash, including on
Windows, so the single ./gradlew line works everywhere instead of
needing a separate gradlew.bat step. And fail-fast is off, so one
platform failing does not cancel the others and hide whether the failure
was platform specific, which is the main question a three-platform
matrix exists to answer.

commitResults.messageTitle: Add a sort command that orders tasks by date
commitResults.messageBody:
Bibi could find tasks by keyword and show what fell on a given date, but
had no way to answer the question a task list is usually for: what is
due next. The only order available was the order things happened to be
typed in.

Sorting is applied to the stored list rather than to one printout. That
follows from how the rest of Bibi works: task numbers come from the
list, and mark, unmark and remove all use them, so an order that existed
only in a past printout would leave those numbers pointing at the wrong
tasks. The sorted order is saved and survives into the next session.

Each task type answers what moment it sorts by. A deadline gives its due
time, an event gives its start, since that is when the user must be
ready for it, and a ToDo gives nothing. That last case is an empty
Optional rather than an invented date, which is what lets undated tasks
be placed deliberately: they go last, because burying dated tasks under
undated ones would defeat the point of sorting.

The sort is stable, so tasks sharing a moment, and the undated ones at
the end, stay in the order they were added.

Two supporting changes. TaskDateTime gains an EARLIEST_FIRST comparator
built on the same whole-day-counts-as-midnight rule isBefore already
used, offered as a comparator rather than by implementing Comparable,
because two values standing for the same moment are not otherwise equal.
Command gains showAllTasks, so the new command and ListCommand share one
copy of the numbering rather than growing a second.

The user guide is rewritten alongside this, not just extended. It still
claimed dates were "treated as text", which stopped being true when
parsing was made strict, and it documented neither find, on, remove,
help, nor the GUI.

Verified: 101 JUnit tests, 19 UI tests including one that restarts Bibi
to confirm the order was saved, and checkstyle clean.

Peer review on the iP pull request found several things checkstyle
cannot catch, because naming quality and comment wording are not
mechanically checkable. All of them were violations of the coding
standard this project already committed to.

Task's completion flag was named complete, a bare adjective, when the

of one idea. Task now matches Storage.

Parser's local holding the lower-cased input was called command, which
is also the name of a class this file returns instances of; a reader had
to work out which was meant. It is now lowerCasedInput, which says what
it holds rather than what it is for.

silently omitting remove and help. Someone who had forgotten remove
would have been told, in effect, that it did not exist.

American spelling the standard specifies, a stray second blank line
after Parser's private constructor removed, and Parser marked final, so
the class cannot be extended as well as not instantiated.

a verb phrase, but both are wider renames worth deciding deliberately
rather than folding into a fix commit.

commitResults.messageTitle: Handle the input mistakes users actually make
commitResults.messageBody:
Feeding a list of plausible mistakes through the running chatbot turned
up several that were handled badly rather than not at all, which is
worse: the user was told something misleading instead of nothing.

A tab between a command and its argument was read as an unknown command,
because the parser looked for a literal space. It now splits on any run
of whitespace, so a tab or a double space is read as meant. Descriptions
have their inner spacing collapsed, which also makes "read    book" and
"read book" the same task rather than two.

Supplying /by or /to twice was the worst of them. The parser took the
first marker and swept the rest into the date, so "deadline report /by
Monday /by Tuesday" complained that "Monday /by Tuesday" was not a
readable date. Repeated parameters are now counted and reported for what
they are. An event whose /to precedes its /from is told so, instead of
receiving the generic syntax reminder.

Commands that take no argument silently ignored anything after them, so
"list done" showed the whole list and looked like a filter that had
worked. They now say what they found and that they take nothing.

Task numbers below one reported that the task did not exist, which is
true but unhelpful; the numbering is what the user has misunderstood,
and the message now says so. A number that will not parse is quoted back
rather than described only in the abstract.

Adding a task identical to one already stored now points at the existing
one and changes nothing. Completion state is excluded from that
comparison: a task already ticked off is still the same task, and
someone re-adding it has lost track rather than wanting two copies.

Storage gains one guard: a folder sitting where the save file belongs
used to surface as a bare FileSystemException naming neither the file
nor the cause.

Verified: 115 JUnit tests and 22 UI tests, three of the latter added for
the repeated parameter, the stray argument and the duplicate task.
Checkstyle clean.

commitResults.messageTitle: Give Bibi a voice and a look of its own
commitResults.messageBody:
Bibi was already named and already had a robot for a face, but it spoke
in the flat template wording every Duke starts with, and the window was
default JavaFX with a picture stuck on it. Nothing about either said
which chatbot this was.

The character it now has follows from what it already looked like: a
small, earnest filing robot that likes keeping things in order. It comes
online rather than greeting, logs work rather than adding it, ticks
tasks off, and powers down with everything filed.

Error messages are deliberately left plain. A personality that garbles
the one sentence explaining what went wrong is a personality bought at
the user's expense, and the whole point of the wording is that someone
stuck can act on it. Bibi is warm where warmth costs nothing and factual
where it matters.

The palette is taken from Bibi's own avatar rather than picked freshly,
so the app looks like the robot it is. The six colours are declared once
as looked-up colours in a stylesheet, so re-tinting the whole window is
a six line change. The window also carries the name in its title bar and
Bibi's face as its icon, which is what appears in a taskbar.

One real fix came out of this pass. The confirmation after adding a task
said "Now you have 1 tasks in the list", which is the kind of small
wrongness that makes software feel unfinished. Counts now go through a
helper that picks the right plural, and a test pins the singular case.

opened under a virtual display to check the palette renders.

commitResults.messageTitle: Lay the conversation out as a person talking to a tool
commitResults.messageBody:
The window showed both speakers the same way: a large portrait beside a
bubble, mirrored left and right. That is the layout of a chat between

people, and it was wrong twice over. Bibi is not the user's peer, and
the
portraits were eating the width that Bibi's longer answers needed, so a
listing of four tasks filled the window.

The two sides are now shown differently, because they are different.
Bibi's replies run the full width behind a small icon: they are the
content, so they get the room. The user's own lines sit on the right as
a
short tinted chip with no picture at all, since the user knows who they
are and a portrait of them earns none of the space it takes. The same
conversation that filled the window now fits roughly twice as much.

Errors are styled apart. A rejected command used to look exactly like a
confirmation, so the one reply the user has to act on was the hardest to
pick out when scrolling back. It now carries a tinted background and a
rule down its left edge, which is findable at a glance rather than only
readable. Making that possible is why getResponse returns a Reply rather
than a String: the window should not have to guess at the meaning of a
message by reading its words.

Resizing works properly rather than merely being allowed. Bibi's text
reflows into whatever width it is given, while the user's chips are
capped at a fraction of the window so they stay chips instead of
stretching into banners.

commitResults.messageTitle: Cover Ui and every command with unit tests
commitResults.messageBody:
Two parts of the program had no unit tests at all. Ui was skipped
originally as console output, which stopped being true when capture mode
arrived for the GUI: everything it says is now readable from a test. The
command classes were only ever exercised through Bibi end to end, so a
failure in one of them surfaced as a failed sentence rather than as a
failed command.

UiTest covers the capture mechanism itself, which is the part the whole
GUI rests on: that a capture must be started before its text is taken,
that starting a new one clears what the last left behind, and that the
error flag is set by showError and cleared by the next capture. It also
pins the wording that other things depend on, including both plurals of
the task count.

CommandTest runs each command against a real task list and reads back
both what it said and what it changed. That covers the cases worth
holding still: find and on keeping each match's number from the full
list, sort placing undated tasks last, add refusing a duplicate without
touching the list, and a save failure being reported while the change
itself survives in memory.

Writing them found a real bug. Captured replies were trimmed with strip,
which removes leading whitespace from the first line as well as blank
lines at the ends. Any reply opening with an indented detail line lost
that indent. Blank lines at either end are now trimmed without touching
the indentation of the first real line.

The four JavaFX classes are left to manual testing, as the increment
allows. They need a display and a running toolkit, and what they are
worth checking for is how they look, which an assertion cannot see.

It is rewritten for someone who has just downloaded the JAR and wants to
use it. Each feature is introduced by what it is for rather than by its

that would otherwise look arbitrary are explained where the user meets
them: why sorting is kept rather than shown once, and why find and on
report each match under its number from the full list.

The errors have a section of their own. They are part of using the
product, not a footnote to it. The guide says what Bibi will tell you
when a command is wrong so that the message is recognised rather than
puzzled over.

are listed because the course requires it, and the use of AI is recorded
there rather than in comments because it was widespread rather than
localised, which is what the reuse policy asks for in that case.

although the parser otherwise accepts any whitespace between words.

commitResults.messageTitle: Give each task type its own add confirmation
commitResults.messageBody:
Every added task was confirmed with the same line, which told the user
nothing the task display below it did not already say. The three types
ask different things of the user, and the confirmation is the one place
that difference can be named without adding a line to the reply.

A ToDo now answers with "Do or do not. There is no try", because nothing
but the user will move it on. A deadline keeps the existing line, which
is about the division of labor and only ever fitted the dated case. An
event notes that it starts whether or not the user is ready, which is
what separates it from a task that can quietly be postponed.

The wording is chosen per type by overriding a method on Task rather
than by testing the type in AddCommand, so a fourth task type would
supply its own line instead of extending a conditional. Each line ends
with a colon because the task itself is printed below it.

commitResults.messageTitle: Restyle the window as a neon terminal
commitResults.messageBody:
The window read as a dark editor theme rather than as a product with a
look of its own: a grey-blue ground, a filled yellow button, and accents
chosen for contrast rather than for character.

The palette is now built around two lit accents on a near-black blue
ground. Cyan marks the machine's own surfaces, magenta the user and
whatever currently holds focus, so the two sides of the conversation are
told apart by colour as well as by position. Surfaces are outlined
rather than filled, which suits a screen better than a chat app.

Glow is applied only to the controls that are meant to look lit. The
transcript is deliberately left unlit: a glow behind a paragraph costs
legibility, and the replies are the one thing that cannot afford it.

Errors move from red to amber. Red now sits too close to magenta to be
read as a warning at a glance, while amber belongs to neither accent, so
an error cannot be mistaken for either side of an ordinary exchange. The
left-edge rule that makes an error findable when scrolling back is kept.

Restore the checks the delete alias left failing
commitResults.messageBody:
Adding the delete alias reordered the imports in Parser and Ui, putting
this project's own packages ahead of the standard library ones, which
is the order Checkstyle's CustomImportOrder rejects. Two lines also ran
past the 120-character limit, one test still asserted the help wording
that the same commit had changed, and the new help entry kept the old
padding, so it sat seven characters right of every line around it.

Put the imports back, bring the long lines under the limit, align the
entry, and move the assertion and the scripted plan to the wording the
help now prints.

Add the error-path tests that hold the alias to its contract: a
task-number error has to name the word the user typed, not whichever of
remove and delete is written into the parser. Both spellings are
checked, each ruling out the other, across the two branches that word
the message differently. The help tests now look for the entry verbatim,
since a bare "delete" was already satisfied by the description
beside it.

commitResults.messageTitle: Fix the command table and setup list in the guides
commitResults.messageBody:
The command summary in the user guide wrote the alias as a pipe between
two code spans. A pipe ends a table cell whether or not it sits inside
backticks, so that row parsed as four columns in a three-column table
and rendered wrongly on the published site.

Name the two spellings in words instead. Show them on separate lines in
the example block as well: joined by OR they read as one long command
to type rather than as a choice between two.

Put the Intellij sub-steps back to numbers. GitHub Markdown takes only
digits as ordered list markers, so a., b. and c. were printed literally
rather than as a nested list.

commitResults.messageTitle: Separate reading a line from choosing a command
commitResults.messageBody:
Parser.parse ran to forty lines because it did two jobs at two levels of
detail: deciding whether a line was usable and splitting it, then
mapping the command word to a command. The second job is one entry per
command word and grows with every command added, so the first was
steadily harder to find at the top of it.

Move the dispatch into toCommand, leaving parse with the work of
reading a line. Neither has changed what it does, and the unknown-word
message still quotes the word in the case the user typed it in, rather
than the lowercased copy used to match.
